617.title: the ashoka grove
617.hook: before dawn the most powerful king in the world walks into the garden, and Sita answers him through a blade of grass
617.howItsDone: Sita's blade of grass appears in Hindu storytelling and devotional art, and in some recitations of the Sundara Kanda her reply to Ravana is read slowly and with great respect.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ashoka, the grove called without sorrow, and Sita in it, a flame veiled in smoke.

Hanuman is still hidden in the tree, working out how to approach Sita, when the garden fills with light and noise. Night is ending. Torches. Music. Ravana is coming, surrounded by his queens, walking straight toward the woman Hanuman just found. Hanuman makes himself even smaller in the leaves and holds perfectly still. And Sita, seeing who it is, pulls her knees up and wraps her arms around herself.
screen: `TORCHES BEFORE DAWN.` → `RAVANA COMES TO THE GROVE.` → `SITA DRAWS IN.`

segments.voice: Ravana speaks first, a long, smooth speech. He praises her beauty. He offers her everything: his kingdom, his wealth, the place of chief queen above all his wives. Forget Rama, he says, a beggar in the forest; you'll never see him again. Before Sita answers, she does something small. She places a blade of grass between herself and him. In Sanskrit, tṛṇam antarataḥ kṛtvā: putting a blade of grass in between. Readers take that gesture several ways. That she won't address him directly. That a stranger is worth no more to her than a blade of grass. That even something as thin as grass is a wall he cannot cross. Valmiki doesn't explain it; he just lets her do it. Then her words are firm. Turn your heart to your own wives. I belong to Rama the way light belongs to the sun. Give me back to him, and make him your friend, if you want to live. Ravana answers with a threat. He gives her two months; if she still refuses, she will die. Then he storms off, and the rakshasi guards close in to frighten her into agreeing. All the while, Hanuman is in the branches, hearing every word. Now he knows how Sita answers power: not with force, which she doesn't have, but with a blade of grass and a sentence that does not bend.
screen: `RAVANA OFFERS EVERYTHING.` · `A BLADE OF GRASS BETWEEN THEM.` · `AS LIGHT BELONGS TO THE SUN.` · then, large: `TWO MONTHS.`

Breathe in and feel the boundary there; breathe out and let it be quiet rather than loud. Steady as grass in still air.

618.title: Sita found
618.hook: how do you speak to a frightened captive from a tree without making her scream? Hanuman thinks it through, and then tells her a story
618.howItsDone: Some teachers of the Sundara Kanda point to Hanuman's choice of plain speech and his soft retelling of Rama's story as a model of how to speak with care.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ashoka grove. Ravana's offer, a blade of grass between them, and a deadline of two months.

Ravana has gone. The guards have finished threatening her and drawn back. Sita sits alone at the foot of the tree, worn out, close to the end of hope. Hanuman is right above her. He has found her, and now he faces a delicate problem. A monkey suddenly dropping out of a tree and talking, in the middle of the enemy's garden, could terrify her. If she cries out, the guards wake, and everything is lost.
screen: `SITA, ALONE, NEAR THE END OF HOPE.` → `HANUMAN, RIGHT ABOVE HER.` → `ONE CRY AND IT'S LOST.`

segments.voice: So once again Valmiki lets us hear Hanuman think. If I speak to her in polished Sanskrit, the way a learned priest would, she'll think I'm Ravana in disguise. Ravana has fooled her once already, dressed as a holy man; that's how he took her. So I'll speak plain, everyday language, the speech of ordinary people, and every word will mean something. And I won't start with myself. I'll start with Rama. He doesn't call out or announce himself. Softly, from the branches, he begins to tell a story, as if to no one. There was a king called Dasharatha, righteous and great. His eldest son Rama was sent into the forest with his wife and his brother. In the forest, his wife Sita was carried off. Rama searched for her, made friends with the monkey king Sugriva, and sent monkeys in every direction to find her. And I, he says, crossed the ocean, and I have seen her. That's all. A story told quietly in the dark, about her own life, by someone who obviously loves the one she loves. Look at the order he chose. She hears her husband's name before anything frightening. She recognizes her own story before she sees the teller. She gets to come toward the voice, instead of having it come at her. Sita, at the foot of the tree, lifts her head.

619.title: Sita found
619.hook: Sita sees a monkey in the branches and wonders if she's dreaming, then remembers she hasn't slept
619.howItsDone: The first meeting of Sita and Hanuman is among the best-loved passages of the Sundara Kanda, and in many recitations Hanuman's description of Rama is read as a devotional portrait in its own right.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita found, and your line, Rama's name first. Hanuman chose plain words and told Rama's story softly from the branches.

Sita hears her own story drifting down from the tree. She looks up into the leaves and sees a small monkey, pale gold, with bright eyes, sitting among the white blossoms. When something you've wanted for a very long time suddenly happens, the first feeling often isn't joy. It's disbelief. And Valmiki says her first thought is: I must be dreaming.
screen: `A SMALL MONKEY IN THE LEAVES.` → `FIRST COMES DISBELIEF.` → `I MUST BE DREAMING.`

segments.voice: Then she catches herself, and her reasoning is lovely. You can't dream unless you sleep, she thinks, and since Rama was taken from me, I haven't slept. So this is real, or it's my own longing taking shape. She is frightened and hopeful at once. Hanuman climbs down slowly, bows, and joins his palms. Who are you? he asks gently. Are you a goddess? If you are Sita, the wife of Rama, tell me. Someone has asked her, kindly, who she is, and she tells her own story in her own words: daughter of Janaka, daughter-in-law of Dasharatha, wife of Rama, taken by Ravana. Then Hanuman says: I am Rama's messenger. Rama is well, and asks after you. Lakshmana bows to you. But how can she trust a stranger who appears out of a tree in Ravana's garden? So Sita asks him to describe Rama. Not his name; anyone could know his name. Him. And Valmiki gives Hanuman a long, loving portrait: Rama's eyes, his voice, his shoulders, his walk, his steadiness, his kindness, the way people trust him. Then Lakshmana too. He tells her how the monkeys found the ornaments she dropped, and how Rama held them and wept. Every true detail is a step closer. Her joy is still half fear, like a moon only halfway out from behind a cloud. And Hanuman has one more thing to show her.
screen: `NO DREAMS WITHOUT SLEEP.` · `WHO ARE YOU?` · `DESCRIBE RAMA TO ME.` · then, large: `JOY THAT IS STILL HALF FEAR.`

620.title: the ring
620.hook: a small gold ring with a name on it, given to the one searcher Rama trusted most, crosses an ocean in a monkey's keeping
620.howItsDone: Hanuman presenting Rama's ring to Sita is a familiar scene in Ramayana painting and sculpture, and in some devotional images Hanuman kneels before Sita holding the ring up to her.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita found, and your line, no dreams without sleep. Rama, described detail by detail, until her joy was only half fear.

Back in Kishkindha, the monkey armies set off in four directions, search party after search party. Rama gave only one of them a token for Sita: his own ring, engraved with his name. He gave it to Hanuman. Valmiki says Rama could see that the monkey king trusted Hanuman above all, and that Hanuman would be the one to succeed. Everyone else went searching. Hanuman went searching with a ring in his keeping.
screen: `FOUR ARMIES, FOUR DIRECTIONS.` → `ONE RING, ONE SEARCHER.`

segments.voice: Now, under the shimshapa tree, Hanuman brings it out. I am a monkey, he says, the messenger of wise Rama. Look, my lady: this ring, marked with Rama's name. I've brought it so you'll believe me. Sita takes the ring in her hands, and Valmiki says she is as happy as if she had met her husband himself. Her face shines the way the moon shines when it slips free of an eclipse. Think what that ring has been through. It left Rama's hand in Kishkindha. It traveled south through forests, through the dark cave of Svayamprabha, past the despair on the beach and Sampati's news. It crossed a hundred yojanas of sea, past Mainaka, past Surasa's mouth, through Simhika, over Lanka's wall, through the palace, up a tree. And it arrived. Words can be faked. A messenger could be one of Ravana's tricks. But this is Rama's own ring, the one she knew on his hand. It says Rama is real, that he's looking, that he sent someone. It says, I haven't forgotten you, in a way no speech could. And notice Rama's choice. Out of everyone, he gave the ring to the one he trusted to get there. Some tokens are only as good as the hands they're given to.
screen: `MARKED WITH RAMA'S NAME.` · `AS IF SHE'D MET HIM HIMSELF.` · `WHAT THE RING HAS BEEN THROUGH.` · then, large: `I HAVEN'T FORGOTTEN YOU.`

621.title: the ring
621.hook: with the ring in her hand, Sita asks the question anyone would ask, and the answer is both sweet and painful
621.howItsDone: Devotional readings of the Sundara Kanda dwell on Hanuman's description of Rama's grief, and on Sita's phrase 'nectar mixed with poison'.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ring, Rama's own, marked with his name. Sita held it as if she'd met him, and your line was, I haven't forgotten you.

Sita has the ring in her hand, and now she asks the questions anyone asks about someone far away. Not the news. The person. Is Rama well? Does he still think of me? Has his love grown cold with distance? When a friend comes back from seeing someone you love, those are the questions that come first.
screen: `IS RAMA WELL?` → `DOES HE STILL THINK OF ME?`

segments.voice: Hanuman answers honestly, and his answer is a portrait of a man in grief. Rama can barely sleep. When he wakes, the first word out of him is Sita. He doesn't notice the insects that land on him. He's lost in thought all day, and when he sees a lovely flower, he sighs and says her name. He is wasting away from sorrow, Hanuman says, but he is preparing, too, and he is coming. Now listen to how Sita receives it. What you've told me, monkey, she says, is nectar mixed with poison. Nectar, because Rama hasn't forgotten her; every detail of his grief proves his love. Poison, because the man she loves is suffering, and she can't reach him. Both are true at once, and she won't pretend otherwise. Yesterday the ring proved Rama is real. Today it opens a harder conversation: how he really is. Hanuman could have softened it: oh, he's fine, don't worry. He doesn't. He trusts Sita with the truth, and she holds it, the sweet and the bitter in one breath. There's respect in that. It treats her not as someone to be protected from news, but as Rama's equal in this sorrow, entitled to know.

Breathe in the sweetness and breathe out the bitterness, letting them sit side by side, like nectar and poison in one cup, without one canceling the other.

622.title: her doubt
622.hook: even with the ring in her hand, Sita has two hard questions, and the epic lets her ask both
622.carry: he didn't know where you were
622.howItsDone: Some readers and teachers of the Sundara Kanda point to Sita's questions to Hanuman as signs of her intelligence and strength, and recitations of this passage dwell on her testing of the messenger.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ring opened Sita's questions, and Hanuman told her the truth about Rama's grief. Your line: nectar mixed with poison.

People sometimes imagine Sita as endlessly patient, never questioning, never afraid. Valmiki's Sita is braver than that: she doubts out loud. A woman who has been tricked once, terribly, by someone in disguise, doesn't trust easily. A woman who has waited this long for rescue is allowed to ask why it hasn't come. Valmiki gives her both doubts, and doesn't scold her for either.
screen: `NOT ENDLESSLY PATIENT.` → `SHE DOUBTS OUT LOUD.` → `TWO DOUBTS, NO SCOLDING.`

segments.voice: The first doubt comes before the ring, the moment Hanuman climbs down toward her. Sita shrinks back. What if this is Ravana again, in a new disguise, the way he once came to her hut dressed as a holy man? She says it to his face: if you are Ravana, playing with me, this is cruel. Then she does something remarkable. She checks her own heart. When I look at you, she says, my mind is glad. Would it be glad if you were Ravana? So she asks him to tell her about Rama; the portrait we heard three days ago starts here, as a test. She weighs the danger against what her heart tells her, and decides. The second doubt comes after the ring, and it's sharper. If Rama loves me, why hasn't he come? He and Lakshmana are mighty archers. Has he grown indifferent? It's the question of everyone who has waited for help that's slow. Hanuman's answer is simple and true. Rama doesn't know where you are. Nobody did, until now. The moment I tell him, he'll come. Her long wait wasn't because Rama didn't care. The world hadn't found her yet, and Hanuman has just closed that gap. Valmiki doesn't call these doubts weakness. They're the doubts of someone thinking clearly in a terrible place, and both are answered not with a rebuke but with information: a description, and a fact.
screen: `WHAT IF YOU'RE RAVANA AGAIN?` · `SHE CHECKS HER OWN HEART.` · `WHY HASN'T RAMA COME?` · then, large: `HE DIDN'T KNOW WHERE YOU WERE.`

623.title: her doubt
623.hook: Hanuman offers to carry Sita home on his back tonight, and she says no, for reasons worth hearing one by one
623.howItsDone: Sita's refusal to be carried away by Hanuman is a discussed passage, and in some Hindu tellings it is read as a sign of her dignity and of the importance of Rama's own victory.

segments.voice: Yesterday: her doubt. Was he Ravana in disguise? Why hadn't Rama come? Your line: he didn't know where you were.

It seems like the obvious ending. The rescuer is here; the captive is right in front of him. Hanuman says it out loud: climb on my back, my lady. I'll carry you across the sea today, and you'll see Rama. In a different kind of story, that would be the last page. Sita looks at the small monkey in front of her, and her first reaction is a doubt so practical it's almost funny.
screen: `CLIMB ON MY BACK.` → `ACROSS THE SEA TODAY.` → `A VERY PRACTICAL DOUBT.`

segments.voice: You're so small, she says. How could you carry me across the ocean? So Hanuman shows her. He grows, right there in the grove, until he stands like a mountain, blazing. Sita believes him now. And still she says no. Valmiki gives her reasons, and each one is real. First, the journey: high over the sea at that speed, she's afraid she'd lose her grip and fall. Second, the rakshasas would chase them, and Hanuman would have to fight while carrying her; she could be lost in the fight. Third, she will not willingly touch any man but Rama. Ravana seized her by force; that she couldn't help. She won't choose it now. And fourth, the one she lingers on: Rama's honor. Let Rama come, she says, defeat Ravana and take me home himself. To be carried off in secret would be unworthy of him. Readers weigh these reasons differently. But notice: her doubt about Hanuman's size was settled in a moment. Her refusal wasn't about doubt at all. It was a decision. That closes a week that began with Ravana's torches and a blade of grass. Plain words from the tree. No dreams without sleep. The ring. Nectar mixed with poison. Two doubts, honestly asked. And now a rescue, weighed and refused.
screen: `YOU'RE SO SMALL.` · `HANUMAN GROWS LIKE A MOUNTAIN.` · `FALLING, FIGHTING, TOUCH, HONOR.` · then, large: `A DECISION, NOT A DOUBT.`

segments.voice: Call up a quick fix someone has offered you, or one you've been tempted by, and without judging it, name its risks quietly, one with each breath, the way Sita names hers. Then ask what the slower way would protect, and let the breath stay even; there's no need to decide.
Her doubt. Sita's doubt that a small monkey could carry her, settled when Hanuman grows, and her refusal, for reasons of safety, choice and Rama's honor.
Your line: a decision, not a doubt. Tomorrow, the goodbye in the grove. That's the week.
